segments.text: You said "libtard?"

segments.speaker: Brian
segments.text: Oh, I've heard that so much. And I went into my local gun shop, where masks should be required, according to the ordinances. And I was in there talking to the kid. He had a pistol on his side. It looked like he was definitely not voting for the same person I'm voting for. And he did not have a mask on. And his dad who owned the shop did not have a mask on.

segments.speaker: Brian
segments.text: Then the kid's-- after I'm in there for a couple minutes, he's like, you don't have to wear your mask. And I'm like, uh, yeah, I'll go ahead and just keep my mask on if you don't mind. And he kind of paused, and he got choked up on, like, he was going to say some stuff. And I was finally like, no, we don't need to discuss it. I just have some questions about these guns. And he kind of wasn't as nice to me after that.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Oh, really? You think you maybe irritated him a little or something.

segments.speaker: Brian
segments.text: Yeah, like, because I was a libtard in his store looking at guns. So I guess now I'm a gun-toting libtard.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: For DeJonae, the moment she decided to buy a gun happened in March. She's a nurse in San Bernardino County, outside of LA. DeJonae has an aunt who wanted her to get a gun for years. Her aunt owns a gun store. It's actually the only Black-owned gun store on the West Coast, where she trains women to shoot. DeJonae is pretty, her aunt told me. She worries about her niece dating and living alone. DeJonae had even had a stalker once.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: But the thing that flipped DeJonae wasn't the stalker. She was in the grocery store after work one day. The pandemic had just arrived.

segments.speaker: Dejonae
segments.text: I've never seen the grocery store look the way that it looked-- lines wrapped around the building, people beating people up for their groceries or for their baskets because there were none. Everywhere. And it was just like complete pandemonium.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Did you say beating people up? Like, fighting?

segments.speaker: Dejonae
segments.text: Yeah, people were getting into fights-- physical fights.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: So wait, what were people fighting about?

segments.speaker: Dejonae
segments.text: The last sanitizer. I mean, but there's not-- it wasn't just one. There were a couple of them. People were fighting over the last pack of tissue, literally the last pack of frozen corn dogs. Everyone was buying everything that they could put their hands on. And I just remember looking at all these people, and it just made me scared. I said, wow, I'm scared.

segments.speaker: Dejonae
segments.text: So I called my aunt, and I said, hey, I need to buy a gun. And she started laughing. And I said, what do you have? And then I sent her the money right there. And--

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Like, online?

segments.speaker: Dejonae
segments.text: Yeah, I Zelled it to her. I Zelled her the money. And I'm like, I already paid for it. This is mine. Put it aside.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: A lot of first-time gun owners I talked to explain their reason this way. They had started to feel something weird in the air, a kind of amorphous anxiety.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Shane is 49. He has a house in the hills in Northern California. So in addition to all the coronavirus strangeness, they've also had wildfires and rolling blackouts. One day, a few months ago, the power went out. And it didn't come back for 14 days, which meant no internet. And then the cell towers stopped working.

segments.speaker: Shane
segments.text: So things started getting weird. That's the best way that we can put it, is things started getting weird. People would drive right up to the grocery store. Not park, just literally drive right up and nose first, right in front of the doors for the grocery store, and get out and just leave their car there.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: You mean those sliding doors?

segments.speaker: Shane
segments.text: Yeah. So there was, like, fraying. There was just a feeling. There was just a feeling in the air that was not a good feeling. You could pick up that things were getting kind of weird and were going to get weirder if the power didn't come on soon.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: I asked Shane and everyone else, when you think about needing a gun, what do you picture? Is there a scene that plays in your mind? Nearly everyone said it's night. They're sleeping, and someone dangerous shows up.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Shane's version is people wandering to his house in a disaster, finding it in the woods through the smoke, and trying to take his family's supplies, their food, their generator, the things they need to survive. There's something pre-apocalyptic about it. He's on his own, protecting his home from marauders.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: This is stuff he doesn't think will happen. But at the same time, for months, they've been surrounded by fires, smoke so thick that it can look like dusk in the middle of the day. So somehow, it does seem possible to him. All kinds of things do.

segments.speaker: Shane
segments.text: I wonder if there are people who-- in our community, who resent us because we're successful or for whatever reason, because we're Jews or because we're gay and-- you know. We do have a growing neo-Nazi threat in this country. It's our biggest internal security danger, is the growth of neo-Nazis. And those people know how to use firearms.

segments.speaker: Shane
segments.text: So but my feeling is, if you're on the left or even a moderate, you should be doing the same thing to protect yourself. My husband's been a little out of control with the ammunition. He's purchased, like, 1,600 rounds.

segments.speaker: Shane
segments.text: And I said, Glenn, after a gun battle involving 1,600 rounds, your gun, A, would melt because the barrel would get so hot, you'd have to stop firing after a certain point. And I said our house would probably collapse. It'd look like Swiss cheese. The walls would collapse inward on themselves.

segments.speaker: Shane
segments.text: But he's like, it's just hard to find ammunition for this gun. And I'm like, I'm fine with about 75 rounds. I don't feel like I need 1,600 rounds of ammunition. And I actually asked him to please stop buying ammunition, but--

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Oh my gosh.

segments.speaker: Shane
segments.text: --he did really stock up. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: OK, I'm trying to picture 1,600 rounds. Is that, like, a shoe box full of bullets?

segments.speaker: Shane
segments.text: We actually did buy some Gucci flats. And that box was filled up with bullets. It's kind of an incongruous look, the Gucci shoe box with the 22 bullets. That's a gay male way of doing it.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Nancy bought her pistol around Mother's Day. She send me a photo of herself on Mother's Day, dressed in a Lilly Pulitzer blouse and pale blue cardigan, holding a Smith and Wesson 380 EZ. She's 53. She owns a small business making luggage tags. She's also worked as a nurse a lot in hospice.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: She lives with her family just outside of Appleton, Wisconsin. She described her town to me as your typical, don't-have-to-lock-your-door suburb. Before this year, she'd never even held a gun. It was actually kind of hard for her to explain why it felt so urgent.

segments.speaker: Nancy
segments.text: It's kind of like a nameless, faceless feeling that I have, almost like the earthquake that the world had where everything shifted. And the normal that we knew is no longer there. It's like the axis. The world fell off its axis.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Since the pandemic, she says, her world has suddenly shrunken to just her family and her home.

segments.speaker: Nancy
segments.text: That was all you had. And so if someone was going to come into your house and take that away, as everything else had been taken away, that was not OK.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Nancy lives two hours north of Kenosha, Wisconsin, where there were big protests after the shooting of Jacob Blake by police officers. Some demonstrators set cars and buildings on fire. The National Guard was called in. A teenager, a Trump supporter who came to the protests in support of Blue Lives Matter, shot three people, killing two of them. There have been protests in Appleton near where Nancy lives.

segments.speaker: Nancy
segments.text: It's this small town. Nothing happens. Nothing goes on. We don't have any murderers, but we had rioters here in Appleton. So we've got kind of a small town taste of people being upset and being-- the tension.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: The police in Appleton don't use the word "riot" to describe what happened there. One man was assaulted, but there were no fires, no vandalism. And when Nancy and I talked about it more, she agreed that riot wasn't the right word.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Nancy already owned her gun by the time this happened, but a lot of gun store owners have said that customers point to the protests as one of the reasons they felt so worried.

segments.speaker: Nancy
segments.text: I don't want to sound like a privileged white woman, that I'm living in this la-la land, which is really mostly white people here. I mean, this is almost Utah white. It's white, white here. But there has been more racial tension and more people coming in. And I don't know. I think it's the underlying fear. And I don't know who I'm afraid of. That's also kind of upsetting, too, is, I don't really know who am I afraid of. Who am I worried about?

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Tell me more about that. What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Nancy
segments.text: I don't know. Is there somebody that's going to be coming for revenge because I'm Caucasian? Is there somebody that's coming for my property? Is there someone coming just because they feel like it?

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: So when you're thinking about just the unrest, are you picturing Black people? Because I also know that in Kenosha, it was a white teenager who killed two people. So I'm just kind of curious. Is it Black people? Is it white people?

segments.speaker: Nancy
segments.text: Honestly, if I had to say what I was worried about is-- and this is going to sound truly awful, but I don't think it's so much a matter of a color of a skin, but more of a socioeconomic level of someone that's so desperate that-- things are so bad and people losing their job and people are unable to make their rent.

segments.speaker: Nancy
segments.text: And I think that's what makes me more nervous than particular Black Lives Matter or African-Americans or anything like that. I think it's more just the desperation of people. So the protests and stuff like that doesn't scare me. I think it's more just the world in general that scares me and the unrest and the uneasy feeling than anything else.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: One more person. Elsa lives in a small town in North Carolina. Growing up, no one around her had guns. She grew up in Kenya, moved to the US over 30 years ago. That nightmare scenario that nearly everyone talked about of being woken up in the night by intruders, asleep and helpless, it actually happened to Elsa a couple of years ago.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: The intruders fled before hurting anyone, but it was terrifying. She thought about getting a gun. But she didn't until this year, when COVID hit and when police violence set off protests around the country.

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: I worry not about the Black Lives Matter. I worry about the crazies that are out there that are against the Black Lives Matter movement that could target someone like me just because of the color of my skin. For one, I'm mixed. And my daughter is pale, very, very-- she's got her complexion. She's got Caucasian complexion because, well, my ex-husband was white. And like I said, he's my ex-husband.

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: So my current husband is a Black man. Yeah, so Black woman, white child is an issue. And even worse, I feel worse for my husband because there are a lot of times that he goes out with my daughter. And my daughter is-- well, aside from her nose, she could pass for white. So him walking out with her, I can see someone trying something crazy, you know?

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: I worry in part because of the rhetoric that I see, number one, coming from the White House. It scares me. And more and more as we're getting closer to the election, I'm more and more scared. And I've become so aware now. Everywhere I go, I make sure I have my weapon on me.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Oh wow.

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: So I came from a third world country. Never expected the environment here to be this thick. I feel so much tension. And I fear so much. There's a lot of fear. You've got the extremists. And you don't know who they are. You don't know who they are. But it's gotten a lot worse during Trump.

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: There are a lot of people that all along have tried to blend in, right?

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: Trump came along, and a lot of the people that used to kind of try to blend in and not bring out their true feelings are now bringing out their true feelings. And they feel like they can get away with it. Whereas, before, that wasn't there.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Do you feel like you can see things changing around you, people coming out, kind of?

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: Yeah, well, when you start seeing the Confederate flag all over you, all over around you, that's a big sign, you know? I saw one that was right on the side of the highway that didn't used to be there.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: How does your husband feel about the decision to buy a gun?

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: Uh--

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: He is completely against it.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, he's like-- I had to kind of ease it in. Yeah, 'cause he was not for it at all.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Why not?

segments.speaker: Elsa
segments.text: He is completely against them. He is completely against guns. So I think he's kind of warming up to the fact that I have a couple. But yeah, he's not comfortable-- put it that way. Even when I'm cleaning it, I try not to clean it when he's around because he's just not comfortable.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: The last question I had for everyone-- now that people have their guns, does it help? Do you feel better?

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Again, here's DeJonae, who bought her gun when she saw people fighting over corn dogs.

segments.speaker: Dejonae
segments.text: I feel so much better. I could go to bed--

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Dejonae
segments.text: --at night. Yes, 100%. You have something to protect yourself. I mean, I live alone, but I still sleep with my bedroom door closed and locked. And so--

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Really? Huh.

segments.speaker: Dejonae
segments.text: Yes, yeah, I do. Just in case, to give me a couple of extra seconds, I guess. That's how I see it. So now I'm fine.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Again, here's Nancy from Wisconsin.

segments.speaker: Nancy
segments.text: Oh gosh, yes. Just having it next to the bed. Yep, just having it next to the bed.

segments.speaker: Shane
segments.text: Yeah, there's no doubt about it.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Here's Shane, who worried about marauders and neo-Nazis.

segments.speaker: Shane
segments.text: Being powerless is not a good place to be. It does make you feel more secure. If things really start going downhill, you're like, we can handle this. I don't worry about that anymore, which is nice.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: And finally, Brian, who had so much trouble finding a gun. He finally picked one up the day I talked to him.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Does it make you feel safer?

segments.speaker: Brian
segments.text: No, not yet. No. No. That's an interesting question because there's a gun sitting on my counter, and I got ammo next to it. And I don't know where to put it.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: Brian
segments.text: And I'll tell you, I'm not-- let's just say the ammo is still in the ammo boxes. And the gun's still in the gun case. I'm not in a hurry to put the ammo in the-- what do they call that thing? The-- they call it something, the ammo goes in. It's-- I don't know what it's called. Because it'll hold so many bullets in it. I forget what that thing's called, but I'm just not in a hurry to put any bullets in it. I mean--

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Got it.

segments.speaker: Brian
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, I-- honestly, I really don't want one.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Oh, you don't?

segments.speaker: Brian
segments.text: I mean, I don't. I just-- I almost feel like I just had to get one.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Oh, interesting. Does it kind of suck to have one?

segments.speaker: Brian
segments.text: Yeah, I don't like it. I wish I didn't think-- I wish I didn't think I needed one.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Brian told me he grew up with guns. But they were for hunting and target practice, for fun. He says nobody talked about self-defense. Nobody talked about shooting other people. But that's all anybody talks about today. That's one thing that unites us. We're united in fear of each other.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Lilly Sullivan is a producer on our program. Noor Gil helped her with additional reporting.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [MUSIC - "I'M SCARED" BY LON MILO DUQUETTE]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three, Second Time's the Charm. So maybe you've heard we're trying to hold an election this year with a possible record-breaking turnout that is also during a pandemic, which has led us into a vast territory of, who knows if this is going to work? Reporter Johnny Kauffman has been embedded with the election staff in Fulton County, Georgia. That's the county with the most people in the state and with the city of Atlanta.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For months, Johnny's been given unusual access to the election staff, the people who are responsible for handling the mail-in ballots and the voting machines and all that stuff. He was interested in seeing how things would go this November, partly because they went so badly when they tried to hold the primary during the pandemic back in June. Here's Johnny Kauffman.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: The primary election here was a mess. Some voters asked for mail-in ballots, but never got them. Then people who wanted to vote in person waited and waited in line.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: People shouldn't have to wait three hours to vote. This is beyond ridiculous.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: One guy famously started his cell phone timer running. And by the time he voted, it was 1:00 in the morning. He'd been there almost eight hours and watched all of Curb Your Enthusiasm, Season 8 on his phone. The front page of the Atlanta Journal Constitution said, "Complete Meltdown."

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: The state government was pretty clear whose fault they thought all this was. Brad Raffensperger, the secretary of state, said, quote, "This all lays on Fulton County." He launched an investigation into the county and asked for a new law that would let him take over county election departments if needed. The guy whose job he'd take over if he did that, the man currently running the Fulton County Elections Department, is Rick Barron.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: Whatever Secretary Raffensperger's opinion is, it's his opinion. It's his opinion alone. And I disagree with him.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: It's worth pointing out Raffensperger and the state government are Republican. Fulton County and Atlanta are controlled by Democrats. Rick started working in elections after he quit his job as a middle manager at a bank. He told me he wanted to contribute to, quote, "the betterment of man or something," end quote.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: Rick has this quality that I think lots of people might like to see in the guy who runs their elections. He's measured and kind of boring in public. Like at press conferences, he'll just rattle off stat after stat. But during the primary, beneath that public face, Rick was full of dread.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: I just was constantly-- I've had this constant feeling of stress and that I was failing at my job. And it didn't seem like anything we did, uh, helped.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: One of the things that went wrong in June is that Fulton had these new touchscreen voting computers that were imposed on them by the state. And there wasn't enough time to train poll workers properly.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: But Rick and the Fulton staff say most of the troubles in their primary were really about the pandemic. So many applications for mail-in ballots came in, the email system crashed. And then some of the staff got COVID. It slowed their operations, and they had to close the elections office to disinfect it.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: Then, close to primary election day, dozens of poll workers quit, scared about the virus. Polling places like churches decided they didn't want to be polling places anymore. Tim Cummings is a manager at the warehouse where the county stores its election equipment. He told me at the last minute the Fulton staff thought about just pitching a tent in the middle of an Atlanta park.

segments.speaker: Tim Cummings
segments.text: Get people to vote there. Yeah, I mean, 'cause we were like drowning men grabbing for straws. We got to find somewhere for this to be.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: In the middle of all this, a beloved longtime employee named Beverly Walker died. Everyone had to cope with that. She was 62 and worked in the department for 14 years. Even after she retired, she would come back to help as a temp. Here's Tim Cummings again.

segments.speaker: Tim Cummings
segments.text: I knew Beverly. We all did. We worked with her because they're here every election. There's a picture of her on the wall in my cubicle right now. They went through a lot.

segments.speaker: Staff
segments.text: And Ralph got sick, too. I didn't realize that.

segments.speaker: Tim Cummings
segments.text: Yeah, he was sick, too. We were worried about whether or not he was going to make it. We still had to get a job done. It wasn't easy. And some days, people were just pissed. But they came in, and they did the job.

segments.speaker: Caryn Ficklin
segments.text: I don't really know how to say it. It's a really bad time to make any mistake, because people right now are really unforgiving of anything.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: This is Caryn Ficklin. She runs the mail-in ballot operation for Fulton County.

segments.speaker: Caryn Ficklin
segments.text: They don't care what you're going through, how you're feeling, what's happening with you or anything. It's just like-- you know. Yeah, I guess it is what it is. It's the beast that we have to deal with right now.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: In the lead-up to the general election, the county made a bunch of changes in hopes of avoiding another meltdown like the primary. For starters, 91 more polling places on Election Day, with more training on the touchscreen voting computers for all the poll workers. Nonprofits gave them millions of dollars to help pay for all that.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: But the thing they're really hoping will make this different than last time is that they're trying to get people to vote now in person or in the mail. Rick will tell any reporter who gets within two feet of him that he wants as many people as possible to vote before Election Day. 80% is his goal.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: So a couple of weeks ago, early voting began in Georgia. Rick and his team had been working nonstop through the weekends, right up till the midnight before the polls opened, to make sure the machines would work without a hitch, and the lines would move quickly. When I saw Rick, he was often harried, messy hair, hopping between meetings.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: On Monday morning, October 12, the first day of early voting, I went to the largest polling place in the county. It's actually the giant arena where the Atlanta Hawks play. The team offered it up after what happened during the primary. I wanted to see how things would go.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: Hey, how's it going? I'm trying to meet up with the Fulton County elections director, who's inside. Gate 2?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When I get there around 8:00, hundreds of people were already lined up, and TV crews were camped out. I tracked down Rick near some closed concession stands.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: Wow, you see how many people are out there?

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: That's really like-- hold on.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: Rick takes a call, talking through a black mask with "Vote" written on it in bold white print. He's more put together than usual-- clean shaven, wearing a dark blue suit. It's a big day. Then, an election worker comes up to him. People are trying to vote, but an error keeps popping up-- "Session ID invalid."

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: They aren't working? What, on all of them?

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: They have over 300 voting computers at the arena. Apparently, none of them are working. Rick hurries down some stairs, past empty seats, to the floor of the arena where the voting computers are set up, a jumbotron overhead. Lines fill the hallways of the arena.

segments.speaker: Staff 1
segments.text: Rick, is that you?

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Staff 2
segments.text: Yeah, so the first two people that came down both did not make it through. And so that's when-- and then we stopped people from coming.

segments.speaker: Staff 1
segments.text: I've already got a call into Nadine as we speak.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: A Hawks employee comes up to Rick and is like, what are we supposed to tell the people in line?

segments.speaker: Staff 2
segments.text: From what I understand, the lines are rapidly, rapidly growing.

segments.speaker: Staff 3
segments.text: We stopped processing across the building.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: Rick is on the phone basically this whole time. I've seen him in situations like this before. Everyone around him is wound up, and he sort of slows down.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: I mean, we've tested all these poll pads so I just don't understand how this-- what the [BLEEP] is going on. [SIGHS]

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: He runs up the stairs, breathing hard because of his mask, looking for a county IT employee. Then the CEO of the Hawks, Steve Koonin, comes up to him. This is not the public relations win Koonin was hoping for when he offered up his team's arena.

segments.speaker: Steve Koonin
segments.text: We should not have been put in this position one hour in, where I have to stand in front of the press and tell them why people can't vote.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: Yeah, I know. Well, we'll get it. We'll get it squared away here. These two guys right now are resetting poll pads, so we're going to be able to get--

segments.speaker: Steve Koonin
segments.text: Right, but they have to do 60 manually.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Steve Koonin
segments.text: And that's not fast. And they don't seem to be-- I mean, that's a voter that is literally--

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: Rick and the Fulton staff finally figure out a fix. They have to update a file and reset the iPads used to check people in. The lines start moving. People can vote.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: [CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: It was a small win for Rick and the Fulton staff. Later, the Hawks CEO, Koonin, came up to Rick again. An hour made a big difference. Everyone's pumped up, except for Rick. Listen to this exchange. Koonin's beaming, and Rick is like, this was awful.

segments.speaker: Steve Koonin
segments.text: Well, I will say our recovery actually was faster than it felt.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: All right, well, it just felt like a nightmare.

segments.speaker: Steve Koonin
segments.text: A nightmare?

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: I mean--

segments.speaker: Steve Koonin
segments.text: Why don't we just go proactively talk to the press and knock it out and fix it?

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: Yeah, that would be good.

segments.speaker: Steve Koonin
segments.text: I think it's the smartest thing we can do.

segments.speaker: Rob Pitts
segments.text: Everyone ready? Everybody ready? All right, well, good morning. I'm Rob Pitts. I'm chairman of the Board of Commissioners of Fulton County.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: Pitts tells the reporters and TV cameras how great things are going. Then Rick gets the job of explaining what went wrong.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: An issue I don't know the cause of it yet. There's something with the database on the poll pads that was here. So we apologize to all of the voters and to the Hawks and Mr. Koonin.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: Afterward, Rick walks to the floor of the arena and pauses, just for a moment. It's serene, watching the people quietly vote. Then he heads to his car. It's around noon, but he seems tired.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: I was feeling so comfortable, and I'm watching people coming in, streaming into the building. And I was like-- I was excited. I thought, oh, wow, this is going to be so good. And then that. What a morning. But I don't understand. I mean, some people are complaining that, wow, this is-- I heard somebody say we've got June all over again this morning at these early voting sites. And it's like, we got 32 sites open. In June, it was five.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: There were snags in those first days. Lines did get long sometimes. But Rick felt like things were under control. But Tuesday night, I got an email from Rick's assistant with some scary news. One of the election staff tested positive for the virus, just like during the primary. I called Rick the next day. By then, even more people had tested positive.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: I'm doing a press conference at 2:00. I don't know if you got it, but I've got 13 infections at the warehouse.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: The warehouse is where the county keeps all the printers and voting computers. They've always been worried about the virus spreading there because it's so full of equipment, and it's hard to stay six feet apart. People do wear masks. And one manager even had a barrier in her office so that people couldn't get close. But she still got sick.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: I just don't want anybody to die out of this or be one of those long haulers where they are just sick forever. Hopefully they'll get over it quick. But we've got a couple guys that are sick that are seniors. I don't know. [SIGHS] Kind of a-- I mean, this going to end up being a national story, probably, when you've got this many in an elections warehouse. This isn't like one or two. This is a full-blown outbreak.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: By Monday, two days later, the total was 23 cases. At least one person was in the hospital. All the workers at the warehouse were sent home, except for a few who hadn't tested positive.

segments.speaker: Tim Cummings
segments.text: I'm at the warehouse. I'll be here for a minute. Hold on for a second. I got a call coming through.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: I called Tim Cummings one night. He's the manager at the warehouse who you heard earlier.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: Are you worried about getting sick?

segments.speaker: Tim Cummings
segments.text: Yeah, I been worried about getting sick since March. A lot of my crew scared, but we come in, we do what we gotta do. We're worried about making sure this election happens successfully. So we're doing everything we can to get it done.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: What are you most worried about right now, in terms of pulling off the election?

segments.speaker: Tim Cummings
segments.text: Getting it all done in time. 'Cause right now, one of the reasons I stay so late is I'm like, if I can make everything that they need to do the L&A and program the machines--

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: He's talking about getting the voting computers all ready for testing and then delivered to polling places by Election Day.

segments.speaker: Tim Cummings
segments.text: If I can get all of that prepared before something happens-- before I full out test positive or whatever, everything will be fine. 'Cause somebody else can step in at that point. My worry is not getting that complete. Hoping I can hold out till everybody else comes back, or somebody gets back.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: All over the country, people are freaking out about the election, worried about hacking, violence and intimidation, the supposed voter fraud President Trump keeps talking about. But none of that has been a big problem for Rick and the Fulton staff. Their problem is something bigger.

segments.speaker: Rick Barron
segments.text: Yeah, the virus has been the disruption. I mean, I heard somebody yesterday say, oh, I've lived through the decades of the '60s, '70s, '80s, '90s, oughts and the teens, and now I've also lived through every month of 2020. You know, it's like-- it's almost like its own decade in itself. And yeah, I mean, this has been the weirdest year of my life.

segments.speaker: Johnny Kauffman
segments.text: The county hired some outside help. Rick says the plan right now is just for everyone to work really long days.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Johnny Kauffman is a reporter with Atlanta's public radio station, WABE. His reporting at the Fulton County Elections Department is possible thanks to the Nieman Foundation for Journalism and the Abrams Foundation. As I'm recording this, the total number of election workers in Fulton County that have tested positive for COVID is 25. Two people are in the ICU. Some others have returned to work.
